citations.quote:
The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of [[def-choice-function]]: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets ([[def-countable]]) has a choice function.

Assume countable choice. Let $S\subset S^3$ be the image of a smooth embedding of the standard $S^2$. There is a smooth ambient isotopy $H_t:S^3\to S^3$, with $H_0=\operatorname{id}$, such that $H_1(S)$ is the standard equatorial sphere $E$. In particular $S^3\setminus S$ has exactly two components. Their closures $B_+$ and $B_-$ are smoothly embedded standard closed $3$-balls with common boundary $S$. If $D_+$ and $D_-$ denote the standard closed hemispheres bounded by $E$, the labels can be chosen so that the restrictions $H_1:B_\pm\to D_\pm$ are diffeomorphisms with the same boundary restriction $H_1|_S:S\to E$. Thus the ball identifications are compatible on their boundary and on a common two-sided collar of that boundary.

Assume countable choice. Let $B=B_1\cup_D B_2\subset S^3$ be a supplied smooth boundary sum of two embedded balls along a disk, with corners rounded. In each $B_i$ let $T_i$ consist of one proper smooth arc $a_i$ and finitely many disjoint interior circles. Suppose $T_i\cap D$ is just one endpoint of $a_i$, matched to the corresponding endpoint in the other disk. The union is a one-string ball tangle $T\subset B$. Call such a tangle trivial if it has no circle components and its proper arc cobounds an embedded disk with an arc in the boundary sphere, with disk interior in the ball interior.

Then $T$ is trivial if and only if both $T_1$ and $T_2$ are trivial. In particular, a nontrivial factor makes the boundary sum nontrivial, and a nontrivial boundary sum has a nontrivial factor.

4. Every regular embedded $C^2$ nullhomotopic circle $c$ bounds an embedded compact disk region in $S$. Here a disk region is a compact subsurface homeomorphic to the closed disk, with boundary exactly $c$; its inherited surface structure and boundary are $C^2$. It is unique unless the **connected component containing $c$** is a sphere; in that component the two complementary disk regions are the two possibilities.

derivations.claim: By [F3], the boundary circle of $D$ cuts $S$ into the disks $Q_1,Q_2$ specified in the statement. The embedded unions $Q_i\cup D$ are spheres with corners along $\partial D$. Round them in a product neighborhood of that circle, away from $L$, and use nearby parallel copies of $D$ when considering both spheres simultaneously. Each sphere meets $L$ at its one original point $x_i$ and its one new meridional point near $p$. No other link intersection occurs because $D$ has precisely the one supplied intersection and the rounding collar misses $L$.

Cutting $B$ along $D$ gives two ball sides $B_1,B_2$, with boundaries the rounded $Q_i\cup D$. Here the ball assertion follows from [F1], rather than from an assumption that every disk is already standard. For the sphere $Q_i\cup D$, the connected open set exterior to $B$ is disjoint from it and lies in one complementary component. The other complementary component is contained in $B$, and its closure is a ball by [F1]. In $\operatorname{int}B$ the two sphere complements are separated precisely by $\operatorname{int}D$: a path crossing between their local sides must cross that disk. Thus these two interior ball regions exhaust the cut ball, and their boundaries meet along the copy of $D$. Restoring its collar identifies $B$ with their boundary sum along $D$.

The original proper arc of $L\cap B$ has endpoints $x_1,x_2$ on opposite boundary disks and crosses $D$ exactly once. Its two portions therefore give one proper arc in each $B_i$, joining $x_i$ to the new endpoint near $p$. Each closed component misses $D$ and stays in one ball. Consequently $L\cap B$ is precisely the boundary sum of the two child one-string tangles. Since the original side was nontrivial, [F2] implies that at least one child tangle, say the one in $B_i$, is nontrivial.

The complementary ball side of $Q_i\cup D$ is the rounded union of $B_0$ and the other child ball $B_j$, glued along $Q_j$, where $\{i,j\}=\{1,2\}$. Indeed $B_0$ is outside the original $B$, while $B_j$ is its remaining part; their common boundary disk is $Q_j$. Their link arcs meet that disk only at $x_j$, and their union is the complementary side tangle. This is a supplied boundary sum in the sense of [F2]; its total manifold is a ball by [F1] applied to $Q_i\cup D$. The factor in $B_0$ is the original opposite nontrivial side. Hence [F2] makes this complementary side tangle nontrivial as well.

The child sphere indexed by $i$ meets $L$ twice by step 1.1, has the nontrivial inside tangle from step 3.1 and the nontrivial outside tangle from step 4.1. It is therefore a nontrivial decomposing sphere. Deleting its two meridional cap disks gives the corresponding nontrivial decomposing annulus. This proves exactly the asserted survival under the supplied meridional surgery, without asserting that the child is isotopic to the original sphere.

boundaries.side_tangle: One proper arc plus possible closed link components.
boundaries.disk: Proper meridional disk supplied in one original side; boundary separates the two original punctures.
boundaries.survival: A nontrivial child exists because original cut side is nontrivial; its opposite side contains the original other nontrivial factor.
boundaries.not_claimed: No saddle bound, normal form, individual factor uniqueness, or isotopy to the original sphere.

axioms.use: Inherited from smooth sphere and ball-tangle suppliers.
